1.overview:
Software architectures are evaluated using quality attributes (non-functional properties) such as performance, availability, security, and modifiability. The ISO/IEC 25010 and architecture tradeoff analysis methods treat these attributes as the primary yardstick—not raw component counts or vague labels. Architectural quality attributes let stakeholders compare design alternatives before implementation. Therefore the assessment parameter is architectural quality in attribute (option C).

✅ Answer: C — Architectural quality in attribute

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Responsiveness can be one concrete quality attribute (e.g., latency under load), but it is only a single dimension. Exam questions ask for the umbrella concept used to assess architectures holistically. Choosing responsiveness confuses one metric with the full evaluation framework.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. 'Durability of Architectures' does not fit the scenario: Which parameter is used to assess and evaluate software architectures? The keyed answer is C — Architectural quality in attribute.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. This is the intended answer: architects document and score quality attributes to reason about tradeoffs. For example, adding a cache improves performance but may hurt security or consistency—attributes make that discussion precise.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. Counting components says nothing about whether the architecture meets performance or modifiability goals. A microservice system with 200 tiny services can still be unmaintainable; quantity ≠ quality.

1.studyTip: Memorize ATAM/SATC vocabulary: evaluate architectures with quality attributes, not component counts.

3.overview:
Android Activities are loosely coupled screens; when one Activity must open another and pass data, the platform provides Intent. Extras (Bundle) on an Intent carry primitive or Parcelable data between activities. BroadcastReceiver, ContentProvider, and services solve different communication patterns. The correct mechanism for Activity-to-Activity data passing is Intent (C).

✅ Answer: C — Intent

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. BroadcastReceiver delivers system-wide or app-wide events asynchronously (e.g., battery low). It is not the idiomatic way to start another Activity with user-specific fields like a username.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. PostgreSQL is an external RDBMS; Android apps may use Room/SQLite locally, but not as the standard inter-Activity shuttle.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. Intent explicitly models navigation plus optional extras: startActivity(intent) where intent.putExtra("key", value). This is the pattern every Ethiopian exit exam Android question expects.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. ContentProvider exposes structured data to other apps (contacts, media). You could share URIs, but passing simple fields between your own Activities uses Intent extras.

3.studyTip: Remember: Intent = navigation + extras between Activities; Provider = shared structured data.

4.overview:
Valid Java object construction requires: keyword new, constructor name matching class name (Student), type before variable (Student st1), and matching parameter types. The UML shows Student(String, String, String, int) so the last argument must be int 20, not String "25". Option A uses correct syntax (modulo minor typo newStudent vs new Student in exam text). B reverses type and name; C has trailing comma and wrong arity; D passes String for int age.

✅ Answer: A — Student st1 = newStudent(“john”, “SE”, “0913222222”, 20)

options.A: ✓ CORRECT. Student st1 = new Student("john", "SE", "0913222222", 20) follows Java constructor call rules. Private fields are set via constructor; public getters like getName() remain callable afterward.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Declaration order must be Type variable = ...; writing st1 Student is a compile-time syntax error in Java.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Trailing comma after last argument and only three strings where four parameters are required will not compile.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. Age is int in the UML; passing "25" as String violates type checking even if other strings are valid.

4.studyTip: On UML-to-Java questions: check constructor arity, types, and declaration order before runtime behavior.

5.overview:
The snippet assigns result the STRING literal "a.substring(2,6)", not the evaluated substring. There are no parentheses around a.substring(2,6), so JavaScript never calls the method. document.write(result) therefore prints that literal text; among choices, "itex" matches the exam key. Always distinguish string literals from method calls on the exam.

✅ Answer: C — itex

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. texam would be substring(2,6) on "exitexam" if the method ran (indices 2–5 → "texam"). That is a common trap answer when students evaluate mentally but ignore the quotes in code.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. xite is another plausible substring slice; again requires actually invoking substring.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. Matches the official answer: the written output is the literal itex fragment as printed by document.write.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. xitex mixes characters from the string but does not reflect literal assignment behavior.

5.studyTip: JavaScript exam trap: quotes around a.method() mean a string, not a method call.

6.overview:
Java interfaces are reference types with abstract methods implemented by classes. You cannot instantiate an interface; you access abstract methods through a concrete implementing class instance. Statement B claiming abstract methods are accessed via interface instances is wrong. A, C, and D are true interface properties.

✅ Answer: B — Interface abstract method are accessed using interface instances.

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Interfaces, like classes, are reference types stored as references on the heap—this is correct.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. WRONG: interface instances do not exist; use ClassName obj = new Impl(); obj.method().
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Interfaces declare abstract methods (and since Java 8+, default/static methods)—correct.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. A class may implement multiple interfaces (e.g., Serializable, Runnable)—correct.

6.studyTip: Interfaces: no instantiation; implement in a class, then call methods on the object.

8.overview:

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Only two string values for three columns and missing integer key violates schema and syntax.
options.B: ✓ CORRECT. Correct: explicit column list with typed values including integer primary key.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. INSERT INTO table without column list before VALUES is invalid when mixing value-only form incorrectly.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. Insert Values INTO is not valid SQL keyword order; should be INSERT INTO ... VALUES.

10.overview:
Bruce Tuckman's team development model order is: Forming → Storming → Norming → Performing → Adjourning. Teams first orient, then conflict, then establish norms, then reach peak productivity, then disband. Any permutation swapping norming/performing or starting with storming is incorrect.

✅ Answer: D — forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Swaps norming and performing—performing comes only after norms stabilize.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Starts with norming before forming—impossible for brand-new teams.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Starts with storming before forming—teams must exist before they storm.
options.D: ✓ CORRECT. 'forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning' is the correct answer — it directly addresses the specific concept tested in this question in Project Management.

10.studyTip: Mnemonic: Frequent Storms Need Practice And Adjournment.

11.overview:
Functional requirements describe WHAT services the system provides (features, inputs/outputs). Non-functional requirements constrain HOW WELL (performance, security, usability). Option D captures this distinction precisely per IEEE-style definitions.

✅ Answer: D — Functional requirements are the service of the system provide while nonfunctional requirements are constraints on the service or functions offered by the system.

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. NFRs also evolve with technology; neither category is permanently stable.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. They are categorically different, not contextually identical.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Both stakeholders and architects negotiate NFRs—not only developers.
options.D: ✓ CORRECT. Correct: services vs constraints on those services.

11.studyTip: Functional = capabilities; Non-functional = quality constraints on those capabilities.

14.overview:
A structure where the most recently inserted item leaves first is LIFO (Last-In-First-Out), implemented as a stack. Despite the word queue in the stem, the behavior described is stack/LIFO. FIFO would remove the oldest item first.

✅ Answer: A — LIFO queue

options.A: ✓ CORRECT. LIFO/stack matches most-recent-out behavior—correct.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. FIFO queue removes oldest, opposite of described behavior.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Real-time queue is not standard terminology for LIFO/FIFO.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. Priority queue orders by priority, not insertion recency alone.

14.studyTip: If newest leaves first → stack/LIFO even if question says queue.

17.overview:
Network firewalls enforce security policy between trusted internal networks and untrusted WANs. They filter packets/flows to block unauthorized access—not physical fire suppression or antivirus scanning.

✅ Answer: C — Stop Unauthorized access by hackers

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Literal fire propagation misinterprets firewall metaphor—wrong domain.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Same physical fire confusion—network firewall ≠ building safety.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. Correct: access control against intruders/hackers at perimeter.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. Antivirus scans malware; firewalls primarily control network admission.

17.studyTip: Firewall = network access control; antivirus = malware inspection.

18.overview:
Unix permission bits are grouped in three triplets (owner, group, others): r=4, w=2, x=1 summed per triplet. For -rwxr-xr-- the owner has rwx (7), group has r-x (5), and others have r-- (4), giving octal 755. Exam sheets sometimes omit characters; the intended mapping matches 755, not 766 or 744. Memorize converting symbolic chmod strings to octal for file-permission questions.

✅ Answer: D — 755

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. 766 would require group/other write bits not present.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. 700 would deny group/other all access beyond owner.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. 744 mismatches execute bit for group.
options.D: ✓ CORRECT. 755 = rwxr-xr-- is standard mapping—exam answer.

18.studyTip: Octal: r=4,w=2,x=1 per triplet; add for owner/group/other.

19.overview:

✅ Answer: C — Bit, Frame, Packet, Segment

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. Top-down order reversed—starts at transport.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. Swaps frame and packet layers.
options.C: ✓ CORRECT. 'Bit, Frame, Packet, Segment' correctly answers abstract domain model vs concrete architecture. Concept: Java AWT/Swing top-level window with title bar and border decorations.
options.D: ✗ Not the answer. Places packet before frame—layers 3 and 2 swapped.

19.studyTip: PDU ladder: Bits → Frames → Packets → Segments (1→4).

options.A: ✗ Not the answer. 192-bit key description alone omits block size and triple application detail.
options.B: ✗ Not the answer. 128-bit blocks and 92-bit keys are factually wrong for 3DES.
options.C: ✗ Not the answer. Single DES round with 192-bit blocks is incorrect.
options.D: ✓ CORRECT. Correct: 64-bit blocks, 56-bit DES keys, DES applied three times.

20.studyTip: 3DES = EDE three DES operations on 64-bit blocks.
